home-energy-audit.title: Home energy audits in Charlottetown: EnerGuide evaluations (home energy assessments), costs and rebates
home-energy-audit.description: Book a home energy assessment (EnerGuide evaluation) in Charlottetown: 5 licensed organizations, local prices, Prince Edward Island rebates and what 66% pre-1991 housing means for your upgrade list.
home-energy-audit.lede: 5 NRCan-licensed service organizations deliver EnerGuide home evaluations in Charlottetown. Here's what one costs, what it tends to find in Charlottetown houses, and which Prince Edward Island rebates it unlocks.

sections.h2: What an evaluation finds in Charlottetown homes
sections.html:
Of Charlottetown's 10,405 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 20% were built before 1961 and 66% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. The typical Charlottetown house dates from 1971–1980, and an evaluation is how you find out what that means for yours: the blower door measures air leakage, the advisor inspects the attic, walls, basement, windows and heating system, and the report ranks upgrades by what they'd save.

Charlottetown gets about 4,404 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −19.3°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Charlottetown. That's about 12% more heating demand than the middle of the 70 cities we cover. The more heating a climate needs, the more each fix is worth, which is why the evaluation's ranked list matters more in some cities than others.

In Prince Edward Island, 36% of households heat mainly with a heat pump, 16% with a boiler and radiators, 14% with a forced-air furnace and 10% with electric baseboards; oil is the main heating energy for 28% of households, electricity for 18% and wood for 8% (Statistics Canada, 2023). The heating system on the report shapes the recommendations: a forced-air furnace invites a ducted heat pump, electric baseboards a ductless one.
efficiencyPEI's subsidized home energy assessment costs $99 + HST, booked directly with one of its efficiency partners.

sections.h2: How a home energy assessment (EnerGuide evaluation) works
sections.html:
• Initial evaluation, about 2–3 hours. The advisor measures and inspects the house and runs the blower door test.
  • Report and EnerGuide rating. You get the home's energy rating in gigajoules per year and a list of recommended upgrades with estimated savings.
  • Do the work. Most rebate programs only count upgrades done after the initial evaluation.
  • Follow-up evaluation. A second visit measures the improvement, which is what most rebates pay on.

heat-loss-calculation.title: Heat loss calculation in Charlottetown: CSA F280-12 heat pump sizing for −19.3°C
heat-loss-calculation.description: A CSA F280-12 room-by-room heat loss calculation for Charlottetown homes, sized to the local −19.3°C design temperature: why it matters for heat pumps, what it costs and who does it.
heat-loss-calculation.lede: The heat loss calculation is how a heat pump or furnace gets sized for your house, and the key input is the design temperature: −19.3°C for Charlottetown, from NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Charlottetown.

sections.h2: Why the design temperature matters in Charlottetown
sections.html:
−19.3°C is the 29th-mildest design temperature of the 70 cities we cover. The F280 calculation works out how much heat each room loses on that design day, from the house's actual walls, windows, air leakage and ceiling insulation.

At −19.3°C, a cold-climate heat pump sized to the calculation can carry most of the season, and the number shows how much backup heat the coldest days need.

In Prince Edward Island, 36% of households heat mainly with a heat pump, 16% with a boiler and radiators, 14% with a forced-air furnace and 10% with electric baseboards; oil is the main heating energy for 28% of households, electricity for 18% and wood for 8% (Statistics Canada, 2023).

The National Building Code 2020 requires the heating capacity for a house to be worked out with CSA F280, and its list of referenced documents names the 2012 edition, CSA F280-12. Provincial codes can name their own edition and climate values, so ask your designer which ones the calculation uses.

Contractors who size by square footage routinely oversize. An oversized heat pump costs more to buy, cycles on and off, dehumidifies poorly in summer and wears faster. An undersized one leans on backup heat. The F280 report is the evidence either way, and it's worth having before you compare quotes.

About $150–$400 as a standalone calculation (a September 2026 planning range; quotes vary). Many energy advisors bundle it with an EnerGuide evaluation, which also gives the calculation measured air-leakage data instead of an assumption.

faq.q: Is duct cleaning the same thing?

faq.q: What is ductwork pressure testing?
faq.a: The same thing as a duct leakage test: registers are sealed, a calibrated fan pressurizes the ducts, and the airflow needed to hold the test pressure shows how leaky they are.

Charlottetown gets about 4,404 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −19.3°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Charlottetown. On Charlottetown's coldest days, window glass and poorly insulated corners get cold enough for condensation at humidity levels that feel normal indoors, so winter humidity needs to stay at the lower end of the comfortable range.

Of Charlottetown's 10,405 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 20% were built before 1961 and 66% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Newer houses (22% of Charlottetown's were built since 2001) are tight and usually have an HRV or ERV that needs balancing and cleaning. Older houses that get air-sealed can lose the accidental ventilation they used to rely on.

• Relative humidity in living areas and the basement.

  • How much fresh air the house gets, and whether an HRV or ERV is balanced.

faq.q: HRV or ERV?
faq.a: Both bring in fresh air and recover heat. An ERV also transfers some moisture, which helps keep very dry winter air from getting drier; an HRV suits houses that tend to run humid.

faq.q: Why did condensation appear after we got new windows?

radon-testing.h1: Radon testing and long-term monitoring in Charlottetown
radon-testing.title: Radon testing in Charlottetown: long-term monitoring, kits and mitigation
radon-testing.description: Radon in Charlottetown: Health Canada survey results for the Prince Edward Island region (3.5% above the guideline), how to run a 91-day long-term test, digital monitors versus alpha-track kits, and mitigation by C-NRPP professionals ($2,000–$3,000).
radon-testing.lede: Radon is invisible, has no smell, and is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in Canada. In Health Canada's national survey, 3.5% of homes tested in the Prince Edward Island health region were above the guideline, and only a long-term test tells you about your own house.

sections.html:
Health Canada's 2012 survey found 3.5% of 113 homes tested in the Prince Edward Island health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports About 1 in 5 at or above the guideline (unweighted value for PEI.

The two surveys aren't directly comparable: the 2024 study pooled about 69,000 volunteer tests and more of them were taken in basements, which partly explains its higher numbers. Neither can tell you about a single house, because neighbouring homes can differ widely.

sections.h2: Long-term monitoring: how to test properly
sections.html:
Health Canada's measurement guide asks for a long-term test with at least 91 days in the heating season, when closed windows and the stack effect make readings higher, so the result is a conservative estimate of the yearly average. It recommends testing for 3 to 12 months. Our radon testing guide walks through each step.

Place the detector on the lowest level where someone spends more than four hours a day, at least 30 cm above the floor and 30 cm from walls, and at least 1 m from vents, windows and doors; avoid kitchens, laundry rooms and bathrooms. The choice of device:

  • Alpha track detectors record radon's alpha particles on a plastic film; you mail them to a lab when the test ends. A long-term kit costs about $30–$80 including the lab fee (Windsor-Essex County Health Unit).
  • Electret ion chambers lose charge as radon ionizes the air inside; a lab reads the voltage drop.
  • Digital (electronic) monitors read continuously and show results on a screen or an app, and cost more (Lung Saskatchewan sells one for $189). For a long-term test, Health Canada says to use one that has passed C-NRPP performance testing, and it still has to run at least three months.
  • Continuous monitoring after mitigation: a digital monitor left running lets you watch for changes between the follow-up long-term tests Health Canada recommends.

• Kits can be borrowed through the Provincial Library Service or ordered from LungNSPEI.
  • For a professional measurement or mitigation, search the C-NRPP directory by your Charlottetown postal code; it lists certified measurement and mitigation professionals.

sections.h2: If your level is high: mitigation
sections.html:
Health Canada recommends fixing levels above 200 Bq/m³ within a year, and sooner the higher the level. The usual fix is a sub-slab depressurization system (a sealed pipe through the floor and a fan venting outside), which Health Canada says costs about $2,000 to $3,000 including material and labour and cuts radon by more than 80% in most homes. Hire a professional certified for mitigation under C-NRPP. After a system goes in:

  • A C-NRPP professional runs a short test starting at least 24 hours after the fan is turned on.
  • A long-term three-month test follows in the next fall or winter, done by a company other than the installer.
  • With an active system, Health Canada recommends a long-term test within two years of activation and every five years after that, and again after renovations.
  • Check the system's pressure gauge (manometer) regularly and never switch the fan off. It costs about $50 to $75 a year to run; a replacement fan is $200 to $300.

sections.h2: Rules and help in Prince Edward Island
sections.html:
• PEI requires new homes to include a vapour barrier and a rough-in for a radon reduction system.
  • The province points residents to the Canadian Lung Association's Lungs Matter program (up to $1,500) for mitigation funding.

faq.q: Is radon a problem in Charlottetown?
faq.a: Health Canada's 2012 survey found 3.5% of 113 homes tested in the Prince Edward Island health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports About 1 in 5 at or above the guideline (unweighted value for PEI. Any home can have high radon, so Health Canada recommends testing every home.

faq.q: How long should a radon test take?
faq.a: At least 91 days, in the heating season. Health Canada recommends 3 to 12 months; short tests can't tell you your long-term average.

faq.q: Where can I get a radon test kit in Charlottetown?
faq.a: Kits can be borrowed through the Provincial Library Service or ordered from LungNSPEI. Hardware stores and lung associations also sell long-term kits, for about $30–$80 including the lab fee.

faq.q: Digital radon monitor or alpha-track kit?
faq.a: An alpha-track kit is the cheaper long-term test: it sits for three months or more and goes to a lab. A digital monitor shows readings as it goes and can keep running after mitigation; for a long-term result, use one that has passed C-NRPP testing and run it for at least three months.

faq.q: What does radon mitigation cost?
faq.a: Health Canada puts a sub-slab depressurization system at about $2,000 to $3,000 including material and labour, plus about $50 to $75 a year to run the fan. Hire a C-NRPP-certified mitigation professional.

faq.q: Should I keep monitoring after mitigation?
faq.a: Yes. Health Canada recommends a long-term test in the following heating season, another within two years of activation, and one every five years after that. A digital monitor running in between shows if anything changes.

carbon-monoxide-testing.h1: Carbon monoxide testing and CO alarms in Charlottetown
carbon-monoxide-testing.title: Carbon monoxide testing and CO alarms in Charlottetown: Prince Edward Island detector installation rules and appliance checks
carbon-monoxide-testing.description: CO alarms and carbon monoxide testing for Charlottetown homes: what Prince Edward Island law requires, where alarms must go, and how appliances get checked.
carbon-monoxide-testing.lede: Carbon monoxide is odourless and can kill. PEI's Fire Marshal advises CO alarms outside each sleeping area and on every level, but we found no rule requiring them in existing homes.

sections.h2: The rule in Prince Edward Island
sections.html: PEI's Fire Marshal advises CO alarms outside each sleeping area and on every level, but we found no rule requiring them in existing homes.

sections.h2: Where CO alarms go: installation rules in Prince Edward Island
sections.html:
What the rules say about installing alarms:

  • We found no rule requiring CO alarms in existing homes; PEI's Fire Marshal advises installing them outside each sleeping area and on every level.
  • For new houses, the National Building Code 2020 (Article 9.32.3.9) requires a CO alarm inside each bedroom or within 5 m outside each bedroom door when the home has a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage, an alarm in any room with a solid-fuel-burning appliance (on or near the ceiling unless the maker's instructions say otherwise), and interconnected alarms in a house with a secondary suite.

In Prince Edward Island, the main heating energy is oil for 28% and wood for 8% of households (Statistics Canada, 2023). Any fuel-burning appliance, fireplace or attached garage is a potential CO source.

There's no piped natural gas for homes in Charlottetown, so the usual CO sources are oil furnaces, propane appliances, wood stoves and attached garages.

Single-detached houses make up 44% of Charlottetown's households; many have an attached garage, another reason to put an alarm near the door into the house.

• Alarms next to sleeping areas and on every storey, tested monthly and replaced by their end-of-life date (usually 7 to 10 years).
  • Annual service of fuel-burning appliances by a licensed technician.
  • A combustion spillage test during an energy evaluation, which catches a venting problem before it produces CO.

faq.q: Where should CO alarms go in Prince Edward Island?
faq.a: We found no rule requiring CO alarms in existing homes; PEI's Fire Marshal advises installing them outside each sleeping area and on every level. For new houses, the National Building Code 2020 (Article 9.32.3.9) requires a CO alarm inside each bedroom or within 5 m outside each bedroom door when the home has a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage, an alarm in any room with a solid-fuel-burning appliance (on or near the ceiling unless the maker's instructions say otherwise), and interconnected alarms in a house with a secondary suite.

faq.a: Most have an end-of-life date of 7 to 10 years printed on the unit; replace them by then even if they still beep when tested.

mold-testing.h1: Mould and indoor air quality testing in Charlottetown
mold-testing.title: Mould and indoor air quality (IAQ) testing in Charlottetown: air sampling, inspection and remediation
mold-testing.description: Mould inspection and indoor air quality testing in Charlottetown: when mold sampling is worth it, why damp coastal winters cause condensation, the CMHC and Health Canada size rules for cleanup, and when to hire a remediation contractor.
mold-testing.lede: Mould sampling tells you whether there's a hidden mould problem and roughly where. It doesn't tell you why, and fixing the moisture source is the actual cure. Here's how to inspect a home in Charlottetown, when air quality testing helps, and how much cleanup you can safely do yourself.

glance.sub: or if it keeps coming back

sections.h2: Why mould shows up in Charlottetown homes
sections.html:
Charlottetown gets about 4,404 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −19.3°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Charlottetown. Mild, wet winters keep materials damp, so poorly vented bathrooms, basements and crawlspaces are the usual suspects.

Of Charlottetown's 10,405 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 20% were built before 1961 and 66% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older basements without a moisture barrier and houses that were air-sealed without adding ventilation are common trouble spots.

sections.h2: Mould inspection: when sampling is worth it
sections.html:
Start by looking and smelling: stains, discoloured patches, peeling paint and a musty odour, especially in basements, bathrooms, window frames and closets on outside walls. Health Canada says measuring mould concentrations or identifying species is usually unnecessary.

No Canadian province has a mandatory mould standard for homes. Health Canada's guideline sets no numerical limit: it says to fix moisture problems and clean up visible mould.

Air or surface sampling helps in three cases:

  • You smell mustiness but can't find the source.
  • After a leak or flood, to check that cleanup worked.
  • Before buying an older house with signs of past water damage.

sections.h2: Cleanup and remediation: the size rules
sections.html:
CMHC and Health Canada sort mould by size, and the size decides who should clean it up:

SizeWhat countsWho should clean it
SmallOne to three patches, each smaller than 1 m²A healthy homeowner, with water and unscented dish detergent (CMHC)
MediumMore than three patches, or patches between 1 and 3 m² (32 square feet)Trained help; homeowners only with training and precautions
LargeA patch larger than 3 m², or many patches through the houseA qualified mould remediation contractor (CMHC)
  • Fix the moisture source first: a leak, poor drainage, or condensation from high humidity. Health Canada recommends 30–50% relative humidity.
  • For a small cleanup, wear safety glasses or goggles, an N95 mask if possible and household rubber gloves. People at risk from mould shouldn't clean it and should stay away.
  • Health Canada suggests professional help for extensive mould, especially growth that keeps coming back after cleaning.

sections.h2: Choosing a tester, lab or remediation contractor
sections.html:
Ask any Charlottetown tester which lab analyzes their samples, and look for one accredited under AIHA's EMLAP program for environmental microbiology. Pair sampling with a ventilation and humidity assessment, which finds the cause. For remediation, get two or three written quotes that describe containment, what will be removed and how the area is cleaned.

Ventilation and humidity assessments in Charlottetown · Our mould and indoor air quality guide

faq.q: How much does mould testing cost in Charlottetown?
faq.a: We found no reputable Canadian source for the cost of a professional mould assessment, so get two or three written quotes and ask how many samples are included, which lab analyzes them and what the report covers.

faq.q: Do I need a test if I can see mould?
faq.a: Usually not. Visible mould needs cleanup and a fix for the moisture source. Testing helps most when you suspect mould you can't see.

faq.q: How much mould can I clean myself?
faq.a: CMHC says a healthy homeowner can clean one to three patches, each under 1 m², with water and unscented dish detergent. Larger areas need trained help or a remediation contractor.

faq.q: When should I hire a mould remediation contractor?
faq.a: For a single patch over 3 m², many patches through the house, or mould that keeps coming back after cleaning (CMHC, Health Canada).

faq.q: Is there a legal mould limit for homes in Canada?
faq.a: No. Health Canada sets no numerical limit; its guidance is to control moisture and clean up mould. Quebec has a voluntary handling standard.

asbestos-testing.h1: Asbestos testing and inspection in Charlottetown
asbestos-testing.title: Asbestos testing and inspection in Charlottetown: vermiculite, labs, and Prince Edward Island abatement and removal rules
asbestos-testing.description: Asbestos inspection and testing in Charlottetown, where 66% of houses were built before 1991: what to sample, lab costs, the Prince Edward Island rules for renovation, and what abatement and removal involve if a test is positive.
asbestos-testing.lede: About 6,900 Charlottetown houses (66%) were built before 1991, when asbestos still turned up in insulation, flooring, plaster and duct wrap. A lab test before renovation is the only way to know.

sections.h2: Where asbestos shows up in Charlottetown houses
sections.html:
Of Charlottetown's 10,405 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 20% were built before 1961 and 66% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Vermiculite attic insulation: loose, pebbly, grey-brown or silver-gold granules.
  • Vinyl floor tiles and their adhesive, textured ceilings and some plaster.
  • Duct wrap and pipe insulation on older heating systems.

sections.h2: The rules in Prince Edward Island
sections.html:
PEI requires a competent person to take samples, a CALA- or AIHA-accredited lab to analyze them, and a certified asbestos contractor for asbestos work.

Whatever the rules, don't sand, cut or remove suspect material yourself before it's tested.

A trained assessor takes small samples, and an accredited lab analyzes them; plan on about $50–$150 per sample. Asbestos labs in Canada are typically accredited under NIST's NVLAP program.

Our asbestos and vermiculite guide · Attic inspections in Charlottetown

sections.h2: If it's positive: abatement and removal
sections.html:
Leave the material alone until a plan is in place. For vermiculite, Health Canada says not to use the attic for storage, to keep children out and to seal gaps around the attic hatch, light fixtures and outlets, and to hire professionals trained to handle asbestos if you plan to renovate.

In Prince Edward Island: All asbestos work must be done by a holder of an asbestos contractor's certificate, and workers who handle or remove asbestos need an asbestos abatement course.

Abatement is quoted separately from testing. Get two or three written quotes that describe containment, what will be removed and how the waste will be disposed of.

faq.q: Do I need an asbestos test before renovating in Charlottetown?
faq.a: If the house was built before 1991 and the work will disturb insulation, flooring, plaster or duct wrap, test first. PEI requires a competent person to take samples, a CALA- or AIHA-accredited lab to analyze them, and a certified asbestos contractor for asbestos work.

faq.q: How much does asbestos testing cost?
faq.a: About $50–$150 per lab sample, plus the assessor's visit. Abatement, if needed, is quoted separately.

faq.q: What should I do if I have vermiculite in the attic?
faq.a: Leave it alone, keep the attic closed, and have it sampled before any attic work. Health Canada advises against disturbing it or removing it yourself.

faq.q: Who removes asbestos in Prince Edward Island?
faq.a: All asbestos work must be done by a holder of an asbestos contractor's certificate, and workers who handle or remove asbestos need an asbestos abatement course.

lead-paint-testing.title: Lead paint testing in Charlottetown: at-risk homes, testing and safe abatement
lead-paint-testing.description: 20% of Charlottetown's houses were built before 1961, when lead paint was common. How to test with $15–$40 swabs or a lab, and how to renovate safely.
lead-paint-testing.lede: Health Canada says a home built before 1960 probably has lead paint somewhere. That's 20% of Charlottetown's houses (built before 1961, per the 2021 Census), plus exterior paint on many of the 46% built from 1961 to 1990.

sections.h2: Which Charlottetown homes are at risk
sections.html:
Of Charlottetown's 10,405 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 20% were built before 1961 and 66% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Built before 1960: probably has lead-based paint (Health Canada).
  • Built 1960–1990: exterior paint may contain lead, and interior paint may contain smaller amounts.
  • Built after 1990: consumer paints were virtually lead-free by then.

• Swab kits ($15–$40) give a quick screen of the surfaces you plan to disturb.
  • For certainty, send paint chips to a lab accredited under AIHA's ELLAP program, or hire a firm with an X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyzer.
  • Test before sanding, stripping or replacing old windows and trim.

Our lead paint guide.

sections.h2: If it's positive: lead paint abatement
sections.html:
Health Canada says leaving lead-based paint alone is sometimes safer than removing it, as long as it isn't chipping or within children's reach, and covering it with wallpaper, wallboard or panelling adds protection. Paint that's chipping, flaking or within reach of children is a serious hazard and has to come off carefully; consider hiring an expert before you start.

No province has a lead-paint rule aimed at homeowners, but contractors in B.C. must include lead in pre-renovation and demolition hazard inspections, and in Yukon before demolition. If you do the work yourself, Health Canada's precautions are:

  • Don't use sanders, heat guns or blowlamps: they create toxic dust and fumes. For do-it-yourself work, Health Canada suggests a chemical paint-stripper paste applied with a brush.
  • Move furniture out or cover it with plastic, seal doorways and vents with plastic sheeting and tape, and run a fan blowing out through an open window.
  • Wear goggles, gloves and a good-quality mask, work in 10-minute stretches with breaks outdoors, and don't eat, drink or smoke in the work area.
  • Clean up daily: put scrapings in a sealed container marked Hazardous Waste, follow your municipality's disposal instructions, and wipe surfaces with a damp cloth you throw away.
  • Keep children and pregnant people away until the work is done; Health Canada says there is no known safe level of lead exposure.

faq.q: Does my Charlottetown house have lead paint?
faq.a: If it was built before 1960, probably; 1960–1990, possibly on the exterior. Test the surfaces you plan to disturb.

faq.q: Are lead test swabs reliable?
faq.a: They are a useful screen. For renovation decisions, confirm with a lab analysis of paint chips or an XRF reading.

faq.q: What does lead paint testing cost?
faq.a: Swab kits run about $15–$40; lab analysis and XRF testing cost more and are quoted by the firm.

faq.q: Should I remove lead paint or cover it?
faq.a: Health Canada says leaving it alone or covering it with wallpaper, wallboard or panelling is sometimes safer than removing it, as long as it isn't chipping or within children's reach. Never sand it or use a heat gun, and consider hiring an expert for removal.

sections.h2: How testing works in Prince Edward Island

  • Metals and naturally occurring contaminants such as arsenic, uranium or manganese when a well is new and every few years after, depending on local geology.

commercial-energy-audit.title: Commercial energy audits in Charlottetown: reporting rules and incentives
commercial-energy-audit.description: Commercial and multi-unit building energy audits in Charlottetown: ASHRAE levels, no mandatory reporting rule, and 1 utility or government incentive for audits and studies.
commercial-energy-audit.lede: Offices, apartment buildings, retail and industrial sites get engineering energy audits rather than EnerGuide evaluations. Here's what applies in Charlottetown: no mandatory reporting rule and 1 incentive program we found for audits and studies.

sections.h2: Reporting rules that apply in Charlottetown
sections.html: • No city-specific rule found (none found): No municipal energy/water benchmarking, reporting or building-performance by-law found; provincial rules apply (see rules.provinces.PE).

• Strategic Energy Solutions for Business, Commercial and Community Buildings (efficiencyPEI (Government of PEI)): efficiencyPEI connects applicants with an auditor for a free ASHRAE Level 1 commercial energy audit. Feasibility study funding by annual energy use: $0 (0-100,000 ekWh), $5,000 (100,000-250,000), $10,000 (250,000-500,000), $15,000 (500,000+ ekWh). Upgrade incentive: the lowest of 1x annual savings, 50% of project cost or $75,000 (annual rebate caps $25,000 / $35,000 / $50,000 / $75,000 by tier). Details

• Level 1, walk-through: a site visit and bill review that benchmarks the building and lists low-cost measures.
  • Level 2, energy survey and analysis: where the energy goes, with savings and cost estimates per measure. Most incentive applications use this level.
  • Level 3, detailed analysis: monitoring and modelling for capital-intensive projects.

Ask which level a quote covers. Audits are done by engineering firms and energy consultants; look for a P.Eng. and credentials such as the Certified Energy Manager (CEM). How commercial energy audits work.

faq.q: Are there incentives for commercial energy audits in Charlottetown?

faq.q: What does a commercial energy audit cost?
faq.a: It depends on the building's size and the ASHRAE level. Get quotes that state the level and the deliverables.
